questions.stem: Which process contributes directly to the negative resting potential of a neuron?

options.text: K+ diffuses out through leak channels more readily than Na+ diffuses in
options.why: The resting membrane is more permeable to K+, so more positive charge leaves than enters through leak channels.

options.text: Na+ diffuses into the neuron through open voltage-gated sodium channels
options.why: Voltage-gated Na+ channels are closed at resting potential. Their opening causes rapid depolarization after threshold.

options.text: The sodium-potassium pump moves equal numbers of Na+ and K+ ions
options.why: The pump moves unequal numbers: three Na+ out for every two K+ in. Equal movement wouldn’t contribute to the charge difference.

options.text: Negatively charged ions diffuse freely from the cytoplasm to the outside
options.why: Large intracellular anions generally remain inside. Their retention helps the inside stay negative.

questions.stem: What happens immediately after threshold is reached during an action potential?

options.text: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ enters the axon
options.why: Na+ entry makes the inside rapidly less negative and then positive, producing the rising phase.

options.text: Voltage-gated K+ channels close and K+ enters the axon
options.why: K+ channels open later, and K+ leaves rather than enters. That movement causes repolarization.

options.text: The sodium-potassium pump reverses and transports Na+ inward
options.why: The pump doesn’t reverse during an action potential. It continues moving Na+ out and K+ in.

options.text: Ligand-gated calcium channels release Ca2+ into the synaptic cleft
options.why: Presynaptic Ca2+ channels are voltage-gated, and Ca2+ enters the terminal. It doesn’t carry the signal across the cleft.

questions.stem: Which event is mainly responsible for repolarization of an axon membrane?

options.text: K+ exits through voltage-gated potassium channels
options.why: Loss of positive K+ charge makes the inside negative again after the action-potential peak.

options.text: Na+ exits through voltage-gated sodium channels
options.why: Voltage-gated Na+ channels allow Na+ inward during depolarization. They then inactivate.

options.text: Ca2+ enters through presynaptic calcium channels
options.why: That happens at an axon terminal and triggers neurotransmitter release. It doesn’t repolarize the axon.

options.text: Cl− leaves through ligand-gated chloride channels
options.why: Inhibitory signalling can involve Cl− entering a postsynaptic cell. That isn't the main repolarizing event.

questions.stem: How does an action potential in one axon region cause the next region to reach threshold?

options.text: Na+ entering the first region produces local current that depolarizes the adjacent membrane
options.why: Positive charge spreads inside the axon toward the resting region, where it can open voltage-gated Na+ channels.

options.text: Neurotransmitter diffuses inside the axon and binds to receptors in the next region
options.why: Neurotransmitters cross synaptic clefts between cells. Propagation within an axon uses local electrical currents.

options.text: The sodium-potassium pump carries the action potential toward the axon terminal
options.why: The pump maintains ion gradients over time. It doesn’t transport an action potential along the axon.

options.text: K+ entering the first region raises the membrane potential in the adjacent region
options.why: K+ mainly leaves during repolarization. Na+ entry supplies the positive charge driving the local current.

questions.stem: Why is transmission across a typical chemical synapse one-way?

options.text: Vesicles release neurotransmitter presynaptically, while matching receptors are located postsynaptically
options.why: The unequal placement of release machinery and receptors gives the synapse its direction.

options.text: Neurotransmitters can diffuse across the synaptic cleft in only one physical direction
options.why: Diffusion itself has no built-in forward direction. The different structures on the two membranes create directionality.

options.text: Calcium ions repel neurotransmitter away from the postsynaptic membrane after release
options.why: Ca2+ triggers vesicle fusion inside the presynaptic terminal. It doesn’t repel neurotransmitter across the gap.

options.text: Action potentials can enter axon terminals but cannot occur in postsynaptic neurons
options.why: Postsynaptic neurons can produce action potentials if their membrane reaches threshold. The asymmetrical synapse is what controls direction.

questions.stem: What is the role of Ca2+ at a presynaptic terminal?

options.text: It enters and triggers fusion of neurotransmitter-containing vesicles with the membrane
options.why: Depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and incoming Ca2+ acts as the signal for exocytosis.

options.text: It crosses the cleft and depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane directly
options.why: The neurotransmitter crosses the cleft. Ca2+ acts inside the presynaptic terminal before release.

options.text: It breaks neurotransmitter molecules down after receptor binding
options.why: Enzymes or reuptake mechanisms remove neurotransmitters. Ca2+ triggers their release.

options.text: It restores the resting potential by leaving through potassium channels
options.why: K+ exit drives repolarization. Ca2+ has a different role at the presynaptic terminal.

questions.stem: Acetylcholine opens receptor channels and produces a small depolarization below threshold. What has occurred?

options.text: An excitatory postsynaptic potential
options.why: An EPSP is a graded depolarization that makes an action potential more likely without guaranteeing one.

options.text: A complete action potential
options.why: Threshold wasn’t reached, so the all-or-nothing opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels didn’t occur.

options.text: An inhibitory postsynaptic potential
options.why: An IPSP hyperpolarizes the membrane and moves it farther from threshold. This membrane was depolarized.

options.text: A resting membrane potential
options.why: The potential changed in response to neurotransmitter. Resting potential describes the baseline before that change.

questions.stem: Why does myelination increase action-potential conduction speed?

options.text: Current spreads beneath myelin, and action potentials are regenerated at nodes of Ranvier
options.why: Myelin reduces ion movement between nodes, so depolarization reaches the next node rapidly.

options.text: Action potentials travel through myelin without requiring ion movement in the axon
options.why: The current travels in the axon, not through the myelin. Ion movement still regenerates action potentials at nodes.

options.text: Myelin increases neurotransmitter diffusion between each neighboring section of the axon
options.why: Neurotransmitters work across synapses between cells. Sections of one axon communicate by local current.

options.text: Every membrane region under the myelin contains additional voltage-gated sodium channels
options.why: The channels are concentrated at nodes rather than spread densely beneath myelin. That arrangement supports saltatory conduction.

questions.stem: How does cocaine alter synaptic transmission involving dopamine?

options.text: It blocks dopamine reuptake, prolonging dopamine's presence in the synaptic cleft
options.why: Dopamine remains available to bind postsynaptic receptors, so its effect lasts longer.

options.text: It prevents synaptic vesicles from releasing dopamine into the synaptic cleft
options.why: That would reduce dopamine signalling at the release stage. Cocaine acts mainly by blocking reuptake.

options.text: It breaks dopamine down before the neurotransmitter reaches its receptor
options.why: That would shorten dopamine signalling. Cocaine causes dopamine to remain in the cleft.

options.text: It closes every dopamine receptor channel on the postsynaptic membrane
options.why: Cocaine doesn't work by closing all postsynaptic receptors. Its key syllabus mechanism is reuptake inhibition.

questions.stem: Which change would make a postsynaptic action potential less likely?

options.text: Cl− enters and hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic membrane
options.why: The inside becomes more negative, increasing the depolarization needed to reach threshold.

options.text: Na+ enters and depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane
options.why: Na+ entry moves the membrane toward threshold and produces an excitatory effect.

options.text: Several EPSPs arrive close together and undergo summation
options.why: Combined EPSPs increase depolarization and make threshold more likely to be reached.

options.text: Acetylcholine binds to excitatory postsynaptic receptors
options.why: At an excitatory cholinergic synapse, receptor activation produces an EPSP rather than hyperpolarization.

questions.stem: A postsynaptic neuron receives two EPSPs and one IPSP at nearly the same time. What determines whether it fires?

options.text: Whether their summed effect brings the membrane potential to threshold
options.why: The neuron integrates depolarizing and hyperpolarizing inputs. It fires only if the net change reaches threshold.

options.text: Whether the first arriving potential is excitatory rather than inhibitory
options.why: The neuron combines overlapping inputs. The identity of the first signal alone doesn’t determine the outcome.

options.text: Whether each EPSP has the same amplitude as a complete action potential
options.why: EPSPs are graded potentials and are normally smaller than action potentials. Their combined effect matters.

options.text: Whether the inhibitory neurotransmitter destroys both excitatory neurotransmitters
options.why: IPSPs oppose EPSPs electrically by hyperpolarizing the membrane. They don’t destroy excitatory transmitter molecules.

questions.stem: Capsaicin activates channels in a free nerve ending. Which sequence can lead to pain perception?

options.text: Positive ions enter, threshold is reached, impulses travel to the brain, and pain is perceived
options.why: The receptor converts a chemical stimulus into depolarization, while the brain produces the conscious perception.

options.text: Negative ions enter, the membrane hyperpolarizes, and the skin itself produces pain
options.why: The relevant channels admit positive ions and depolarize the ending. Pain is perceived in the brain, not in the skin.

options.text: Capsaicin travels through the sensory axon to activate receptors inside the brain
options.why: Action potentials carry the information to the brain. Capsaicin acts on the nerve ending in the skin.

options.text: The nerve ending heats the skin until temperature receptors begin producing impulses
options.why: Capsaicin can activate receptor channels without raising skin temperature. The burning feeling is neural perception.
